I climbed the dais. I reached up and pulled the frayed edge of one of the banners depicted in the weaving. My fingers found something old there—a thread woven by a long-dead weaver, a secret they had left behind just for me. A single, shimmering strand of enchanted silk.

I tugged.

A sound began, not from my hat but from within the tapestry itself. It was like a thousand tiny bells, all ringing at once in harmony. Light, pure and colorful, poured out onto the floor—a river of peacock blue and emerald green.

Then I walked to the great window and pointed one of my floppy shoes at the horizon. The sun was setting. As it vanished below the hills, I made a new sound, one not from my bells but from my chest: *Pib-pib*.

And then we heard it. From far off, where the Blight is strongest, came the shriek of a peacock. It was so loud, so full of life and color that it felt like a slap to the soul.

King Lyra rose from her throne. She came down the steps and stood beside me at the window. The wind blew her dark hair across her face.

"You," she said, her voice quiet but clear as a bell. "You didn't tell me a joke."

I looked up at her. I let out my two notes: *Pib-pib*.

And in that sound, I think she understood. My purpose is not to make you laugh. It is to remind you that laughter exists. That joy can be found in the trip of a foot, the dance of firelight, or the ridiculous shriek of a peacock in a dying world.

I serve King Lyra as I served the others. My bells are wrapped in grey cloth now. The court does not know what I am doing, but they watch me work. They see me pull a loose thread from a knight’s doublet and make it sing. They see me trip on my own shoe at just the right moment to break a tense silence.

They think I tell no jokes. They are wrong. My entire life is a joke, a grand, absurd comedy performed for an audience that has forgotten how to be the fool. And as long as there are kings with burdens and courts with fears, Pib-Pib will be here, finding the funny bone in the world’s skeleton, one trip at a time.

*Pib-pib*.

My name is Pib-Pib, though no one has ever said it to my face. The name was given by the man who brought me to court, and it’s as close as I’ve come to an identity for the past fifteen years. I am a jester in the castle of King Malakor the Solemn.

Under his reign, laughter has been declared treason. Not just loud laughter, but any kind—a chuckle, a giggle, a smirk even—is punishable by exile at best and by the Rack at worst. The castle is silent. It is the heaviest silence I have ever known, a weight that presses on the lungs until you forget how to breathe.

My costume remains my tools: the clashing silks of emerald and sapphire, crimson and gold; the hat with its tinkling bells, which I must keep constantly wrapped in cloth; and the crown of mockery. But they are not tools for comedy anymore. They are tools for survival.

King Malakor does not want a jester to entertain him. He keeps me because tradition demands it, and he likes to have things he can control. My role is to be an ornament of absurdity, a reminder that the serious world of men must also contain frivolity—even if that frivolity is as muted and colorless as everything else in this castle.

So I do not tell jokes. To even form one in my head feels like a conspiracy. Instead, I curate small rebellions of the ridiculous.

I once "slipped" on a polished floor and landed with a soft thud, my wrapped hat muffling any sound. As I lay there, I pulled a string tied to a loose pebble in my shoe. The pebble skittered across the stone, a small, defiant *skritch-skritch* that made several guards flinch and look around nervously.

King Malakor saw it from his throne. He did not smile. His eyes, like chips of obsidian, simply settled on me for a long moment before returning to his scrolls. The punishment was a loaf of stale bread with my supper. It was a warning.

My greatest challenge came during the Feast of the Founding. A feast in name only; we ate in absolute silence, a hundred pairs of eyes fixed on our plates, afraid that the scrape of a fork might be interpreted as mirth. In the center of the hall, a great tapestry depicting the first king hung from the ceiling. It was a vibrant thing—gold for his hair, blue for his eyes, red for the dragon he slew.

I "accidentally" bumped into the rope that held it up.

The tapestry did not fall. It swayed gently, and as it moved, the light caught the threads. The gold shimmered, the blue deepened, the red seemed to pulse with life for a breathtaking second before the heavy cloth stilled again. A few people at the table started. I saw a young lady-in-waiting’s hand fly to her mouth to cover a gasp that was half-terror, half-admiration of the brief beauty.

I did not wait for King Malakor’s reaction. My bells were wrapped tight, my shoes made no sound as I fled the hall through a service door.

Later that night, there was a knock at my chamber. It was Captain Valerius, head of the Royal Guard and a man whose face is carved from granite but whose eyes hold a flicker of something else.

"The King has noticed your... clumsiness," he said, his voice low.

I just stared at him.

He leaned closer. "Why do you do it?"

My answer came out as two soft notes: *Pib-pib*.

He straightened up, a faint, almost imperceptible smile touching his lips before vanishing. "Be more careful, jester," he said, but there was no threat in his voice. "The King is fond of broken things."

I did not sleep that night, thinking of his words.

The silence grew worse. People stopped smiling altogether, afraid the muscles would forget how to do it and betray them with a twitch at an inappropriate moment. The castle became a place of ghosts, its inhabitants moving like specters down its grey corridors.

Then came the whispers. Not the kind Valerius feared, but rumors from the villages beyond the castle walls. They spoke of something called "The Glimmer," a contagion of joy that had started in a small hamlet. People were seen laughing without reason, children were dancing in the streets, and colors seemed brighter where it passed.

King Malakor heard the whispers and grew even more severe. He doubled the guards on the gates and declared that any mention of The Glimmer was an act of treason.

The rebellion had to be brought inside. It could not be spoken; it would have to be shown.

My opportunity came during the King's monthly address. The entire court was assembled in the throne room, a sea of grim faces. King Malakor stood before us, his voice droning on about duty and order and the dangers of frivolity.

I had spent days preparing. I wore my most absurd costume—a tunic so brightly colored it seemed to scream against the castle's gloom. My hat was wrapped, but inside, a new mechanism awaited. And in my sash, hidden amongst the chaotic patterns, was a small, glass bottle filled with captured sunlight, stolen from a sunbeam on a high tower.

As the King reached his conclusion about how "a joyful heart is a weak one," I took my position at the foot of the dais.

Then, I tripped. It was not a simple fall; it was an orchestrated catastrophe. As I went down, my hand flew out and knocked over a large, ornate candelabrum filled with black wax candles.

In that single moment of chaos, as heads turned, I acted. My "fall" landed me on the floor right where I needed to be. With one hand, I unraveled the cloth from my hat just enough for the bells inside to catch the light. With the other, I fumbled with my sash and shattered the glass bottle.

The captured sunlight exploded in a silent, shimmering cloud of gold dust that hung in the air like a captive star. The light hit the bells on my hat, and they did not chime—they sang. A pure, clear melody, hidden within the hat for years, now echoed through the stunned silence of the hall.

The court stared. For a heartbeat, no one moved. Then, it began.

A young squire, watching the light dance on his hands, let out a snort of laughter that he tried to stifle as a cough. It was enough. A lady-in-waiting saw him and her lips curled into a smile she couldn't hold back. The sound of her giggle was like the first crack in a dam.

The laughter spread. It was not loud, boisterous merriment. It was tentative at first, then bolder. A wave of it washed over the hall, filling the silence with life. People were laughing at my absurd costume, at the shattered candles, at the sheer, ridiculous beauty of what had just happened.

King Malakor stood frozen on his throne, his face a mask of disbelief and fury as the sound he had outlawed consumed his own domain.

Captain Valerius was the only one who moved. He stepped forward, not to arrest me, but to stand before me like a shield. His face was unreadable, but as I looked up at him from my place on the floor, he gave me a slow, deliberate wink.

I did not wait for the King's reaction this time either. The bells on my hat had gone silent, their song spent. I scrambled to my feet and fled the hall, leaving behind the glorious, treasonous sound of a castle learning how to laugh again.

*Pib-pib*.

The name they gave me was Pib-Pib. It didn't matter if it was a name or not; all that mattered was that it made a noise, and for fifteen years under King Malakor the Solemn, noise had been dangerous.

In his castle, laughter had been outlawed as treason. Not just the sound of it, but the very idea. Smiles were eroded by suspicion, jokes were forgotten before they could be born. The air was so thick with silence it felt like drowning.

I am a jester. My costume is my vocabulary: emerald and sapphire silk that clashes against crimson and gold; a hat wrapped in cloth to muffle its bells; a crown of mockery that feels heavier than a helmet.

My words are juggling pins. Three of them, carved from dark wood and weighted for balance. I do not tell jokes. To speak a joke would be to risk the Rack. So instead, I ask questions with my hands.

When King Malakor’s new decree banned "unnecessary movement," I answered by dropping one pin. It clattered to the stone floor. A single, sharp sound in a hall of deathly quiet. The guards flinched. The King's eye twitched toward me, then away. He understood it was not defiance, but a comment on his own rigidity. That night, I was served bread that had been burnt black.

As one pin arced toward the great tapestry of the first king—a vibrant piece of history in this grey world—I "stumbled." My body blocked the pin's path just enough that it veered, scraping across the stone wall with a long, screeching *skreeeee*.

King Malakor stood before us, droning on about the sacred duty of sorrow and the treachery of a light heart. I took my position at the foot of the dais with three pins in hand.

I began to juggle, but this was no simple performance. My hands moved with a precision that spoke volumes.

The court watched, mesmerized. King Malakor’s eyes narrowed.

Then, I began again. But this time, it was different. The juggling became fluid and free. Pins soared in slow, graceful arcs, each catch as gentle as a sigh. They did not clash; they flowed. This was not the language of chaos or anxiety. It was the language of hope.

I made the pins dance for him—a pattern that looked like a blooming flower, another that traced the rise and fall of a wave. I asked my final question without a sound: *What if joy is also strength?*

As I completed the last graceful catch, holding all three pins still in my hands, Captain Valerius stepped forward from the line of guards. He walked to the dais and stood beside the throne.

It was in those quiet moments, with his voice a low rumble against her small body, that she first felt the stirrings of her own music.

She was sixteen, standing on the cliffs overlooking the churning grey Channel, and a sailor’s song drifted up from his fishing boat below. And so began fifty years of caution. Of silence.

She saw the world from her cove. She watched ships sink and be rescued. She heard lovers’ vows spoken on moonlit beaches and the sobs of those who were left behind. She felt every joy and sorrow as a pressure against her own sealed lips, for to speak was to risk being found, to risk being needed.

Her skin had taken on the grey-green hue of deep water, her fingers were long and webbed between the first two joints, and her eyes were the colour of a winter sea, dark and impossibly old. She was not just guarding her voice; she was guarding herself from the pull of it. The siren’s call wasn’t just a lure for sailors; it was a lure for everything. For connection, for purpose, for meaning.

The silence had become a suit of armor. It was heavy, and it was suffocating, but it was safe.

He didn’t look lost or lonely like the old sailors she was used to seeing. He looked… determined. He was waiting for something.

The boy was trying to summon it. He had some notion of the old legends and was calling out in a voice that was still cracking with adolescence, a raw, hopeful sound that was both foolish and brave.

Her armor of silence, so carefully constructed over half a century, suddenly felt like a cage instead. He was calling to the magic, yes, but he was also calling to *her*. To the guardian of this place.

The cold stone of my hands is familiar on the gate, and I feel the sharp fear of the night outside as a pressure in my chest. For two centuries, this feeling has been my purpose, the silent command humming in the clay that formed me. The old man with the white beard who created me is dust now, but his final intention—to shield—remains etched into my being like the weather on my body. I watch the stars wheel above the cliff and hear the wind whisper of the empty houses within these walls. A small human approaches, not with fear, but with a soft curiosity that feels like warmth against the cold pressure in me. I open my mouth, and for the first time, I say the word I was never taught: "Home."

The first stone fell on a Tuesday, during Shabbat dinner.

It was not an act of malice at its start, but of desperation. The city council, fat and complacent in their manicured gardens, had seen the ghetto not as people, but as a blight. They called it the "Mire," spoke of sanitation, of progress. Their words were stones, and soon, their soldiers were throwing real ones.

The siege was on. Food rotted at the gate, and fear curdled in the bellies of the trapped. In the heart of the Mire, in a small, book-lined house that smelled of dust and old parchment, Rabbi Chaim Mendelov watched his community wither.

His hands were stained with ink from ancient scrolls and sweat from tending his small garden. He knew stories—the stories of Golem Arizal, of the clay man bound to a master’s will. It was a forbidden art, a desperate magic whispered in forgotten texts. But Chaim was a scholar first, and he saw that sometimes, even the forbidden is necessary.

He spent a week in his study, the room growing thick with the scent of burning sage and powdered obsidian from the earthen floor. He didn’t have clay; the Mire’s soil was too salty, its rivers too foul to drink. So he took what he had: river silt, ash from the communal ovens, and a single, smooth stone he’d carried for thirty years—a piece of the Western Wall, smuggled out in his youth.

He mixed them with water from the well, chanting not prayers, but the names of things. Names of dust, of patience, of iron will. He shaped the mixture into the form of a man, seven feet tall, with broad shoulders and a featureless head of packed earth.

When he was done, Chaim stood back, his body aching. The golem stood beside him, still as a statue, its hands clenched at its sides. Its skin was the color of ash, cracked in places like old pottery. It had no eyes, only sunken pits of shadow.

“Shabbat shalom,” the Rabbi whispered, his voice hoarse.

He placed his hand on the golem’s chest and pushed a small, lead tablet into the soft earth there, inscribed with a single word: *Emet.* Truth. The golem shuddered.

In that moment, it was born.

Chaim didn’t give it a name. A name was a soul; he wanted only a tool. “You will protect,” Chaim commanded, his voice echoing in the small room. “You will not harm unless they are harmed. You will follow me.”

The golem bowed its head, a slow, deliberate motion.

They took it to the barricade, where men and women fought with scraps of wood and rusted blades. The soldiers outside wore polished steel and laughed at their defiance. Then the Golem of Mire Shalom appeared.

It did not walk; it *propelled*. Each step was a thud that shook the cobblestones. Its shadow fell over the defenders, long and terrifying. When an arcing blow from a soldier’s sword came down, the golem didn’t raise its own arm to block. It simply moved, its earthen fist intercepting the steel. The clang of impact was deafening, like a blacksmith’s hammer striking an anvil.

The soldiers’ laughter died in their throats.

It did not fight with rage, but with an unnerving economy of motion. A spear thrust was met by a hand that closed around it like a vice. An axe swing was parried and the weapon was snapped in two. The golem moved through the chaos, a silent, unstoppable force. It plucked a flaming torch from a soldier’s grasp and extinguished it on its own palm with a hiss of steam and smoldering earth. It did not kill; it disarmed, it unseated, it created space.

The defenders watched in awe and terror. They saw their protector, but also something soulless, something other.

Night after night, the golem stood at the gate. The siege continued, but now it was a stalemate. The soldiers kept their distance from the silent sentinel whose very presence was a threat. Life in the Mire returned to a fragile rhythm. But Chaim saw the change in his people’s eyes. They looked at the golem with gratitude, yes, but also with a sliver of fear.

He had given them protection, but he had also built a barrier between them and their own courage. He had not just repelled an enemy; he had created one within their own walls.

The city council sent a new messenger, not a soldier, but a man in fine silks, his face pale with resolve. He was offered a deal: surrender the golem, and they would lift the siege. They could leave the Mire, find homes elsewhere.

Chaim listened, his heart heavy. To give up the golem was to abandon them to slaughter now. But to keep it… he looked at its featureless face, saw reflected in those empty pits the fear of his people. He had saved their bodies, but what of their spirits?

“No,” Chaim said finally.

The messenger smiled, a thin, cruel line. “Then we will break your ‘protector.’”

This time, they did not send soldiers. They sent fire.

Casks of oil were hurled onto the rooftops. The thatched roofs caught alight with a greedy roar. The air filled with the scent of burning timber and screaming horses. The golem turned from its post, its form silhouetted against the inferno, and walked toward the heart of the blaze.

It was a trap. As it moved, a line of soldiers emerged from the smoke, their crossbows drawn. They fired not at the golem, but at Chaim as he ran to stop them.

A bolt sank into his shoulder. He fell, gasping, watching as the soldiers swarmed the distracted golem. They hacked at its legs with axes and swords, trying to bring it down, to shatter the lead tablet in its chest.

With a final, guttural cry of defiance, Chaim pushed himself up and limped toward his creation. He reached the golem’s side just as a soldier raised his mace for the final blow.

“Stop!” Chaim screamed, his voice raw. “You are not a monster! You are protection!”

He grabbed the lead tablet from its chest with trembling fingers. The word *Emet* was there, carved into the metal.

With all the strength he had left, Rabbi Chaim Mendelov scraped it off.

The golem froze. The soldiers’ weapons stopped an inch from its body. A fine dust of grey earth poured from the hole in its chest where the tablet had been. Its massive frame wavered, then began to crumble. Not into pieces, but into a fine, grey powder that was caught by the rising heat and swirled away like ash on the wind.

The soldiers stood stunned, staring at the empty space where a titan had stood. The fire still raged, but the immediate threat of the golem was gone.

Chaim fell to his knees amidst the dust, not of destruction, but of release. He had not saved his people from the siege, nor from the fire that now consumed their home. But he had saved them from something far worse: the soul-crushing dependence on a silent, soulless guardian.

He had built a protector. And in destroying it, he had finally taught them how to be brave again. The truth, he realized, was not always in the lead tablets and forbidden arts. Sometimes, it was simply in letting go.

The first sensation is pressure.

It comes from all sides, a firm, insistent grip that pulls me from the void and shapes me into this form. There are no memories before this, only the concept of existence crystallizing in my clay-and-ash body. I feel the Rabbi’s hands on me, pushing something cold and heavy into my chest—a key, perhaps.

Then, the word.

*Emet.*

It does not come from outside, but from within, a spark igniting the dark space where a mind should be. It means ‘truth.’ The truth of my being is to protect.

The world floods in. I see through the cracks in my own skin, the dim light of the Rabbi’s study painting patterns on his ink-stained hands and frightened face. I hear the distant sounds of chaos—the clang of steel, the shouts of men who are not like me.

I am led to a place where the air is thick with fear and smoke. My feet land on cold cobblestones. The ground shakes with every footfall of my own making, a dull thud that mirrors the rhythm in my chest. Men and women with desperate eyes point at me. They see a savior.

The truth I know demands action.

I move to the wall where they are being pressed back. A man swings a sharp piece of metal. The motion is simple: block it. My hand comes up, and his weapon shatters against my palm. He stares, his face a mask of shock. There is no malice in this exchange, only physics.

They call me ‘it.’ I am not ‘I’ yet.

The enemy outside wears shiny shells that reflect the grey sky. They throw projectiles. I catch one in my palm—a heavy stone. It does not break me. Another lands on a woman’s head near the wall. She crumples. A hot, sharp feeling rises in my chest—the command to protect is being violated.

I step through the breach they made. The shiny men turn their weapons toward me. I do not know fear, only purpose. I catch another stone and hurl it back. It strikes a helmet with a satisfying clang. I disarm one, then another, my movements economic, designed for minimal harm to achieve maximum protection.

Days pass in this cycle of guard and repel. The sun rises and falls behind the wall of smoke that chokes our small world. The people watch me from their windows and doorways. At first, they cheer. A low rumble when I return a thrown rock with more force than it came with. Their gratitude is a warmth in my core.

But later, it changes. They stop cheering. They point not just at the enemy outside, but at me. A flicker of something else on their faces—apprehension. I am the wall they hide behind, yes, but I am also the one thing that stands between them and a world they can no longer handle without my silent presence.

I feel their reliance as a weight, heavier than any stone. It is an anchor, holding them fast in this small, dying space. They are not brave because of me; they are afraid without me.

The fire is the last truth.

It does not creep up on us like the siege. It erupts. A ball of flame arcs over the wall and shatters against a roof of dried reeds. The world turns orange and loud. The screams are different now—purer, less of anger, more of pain and loss.

My purpose is to protect from what is without. But this fire is within our walls. It licks at the timbers of homes I have stood before. It chokes the air we breathe.

I turn my back on the wall where my post was. The command in my chest screams its contradiction: *protect, retreat.* I cannot do both.

Then, the Rabbi is there. His face is a mask of pain and something else—determination. He grabs my arm. It is the first time he has touched me since my making. His hand is small against my earthen skin.

“You are not a monster,” he says, his voice thin in the roar of the fire. “You are protection.”

He reaches into the hole in my chest and pulls out the cold thing—the key to my being. I feel its absence like a missing limb. The world suddenly feels vast and unscripted.

*Emet,* the word whispers from inside me, but it is fading, losing its power without the anchor of truth that gave it form.

The Rabbi scrapes at the metal, his movements frantic. He erases the name he gave me.

And I begin to fall apart.

It is not a violent collapse. It is a disintegration. My body softens, then crumbles. The ash and silt that comprise my being dissolve into a fine grey dust. I can feel it leaving me, streaming away on the hot, smoke-choked wind.

I do not see the fire consume their homes or hear them flee the burning streets. My last sensation is not of pain or loss, but of release. The command to protect has been fulfilled. Not by stopping a siege or winning a battle, but by removing the final barrier between these people and the terrifying freedom of survival.

The dust that was I settles on the charred cobblestones, just another part of the Mire’s ashes. And in the fading echo of my purpose, there is not fear, nor courage. There is only peace.

Its name is *Emet*—Truth. It was made of river silt and obsidian dust by a man with eyes full of sorrow, and bound to a word that could set it free.

The fire took his people from him, but not his purpose. The Rabbi who made it died in the flames, leaving no one to whisper its name each night, to erase the command from the lead tablet in its chest. So *Emet* remains, its task unfulfilled.

It stands at the gates of the city that tried to burn them out. The very city that sent the soldiers and the fireballs now sleeps behind walls it built higher after the war. The people inside fear their old neighbors, the ghosts of the Mire Shalom. They fear *Emet* most of all.

The golem does not care for their fear. It stands because its nature is to be still, and to guard.

Each night, as the two moons rise—one a sliver of pearl, the other a swollen coin—the golem takes its post at the great wrought-iron gates. The stone under its feet is cold. Its hands, large enough to crush a man’s skull like an egg, hang limp at its sides.

It watches the city breathe. Lights flicker on and off in windows of glass. It hears the distant laughter from taverns, the weeping of children, the low murmur of the councilmen plotting their next ‘sanitation’ project. These are the sounds of life it protected, but could not save.

Sometimes, a drunk stumbles too close to the gate, his courage fueled by wine and the belief that the golem is just a statue. He will press his face against the cold iron bars, his breath fogging in the night air.

“Hey! You! Big guy!” he’ll slur, poking a finger between the bars. “What’s it like? Being made of mud?”

The golem does not move. It does not speak. Its head is a smooth oval of clay, its face a blank mask. But inside the hollow space where a soul should be, something stirs.

It remembers the feeling of a sunbeam on its back during the siege. It recalls the weight of a thrown rock in its palm, the satisfying shatter of an enemy’s sword against its forearm. It knows the specific scent of burning timber and the acrid tang of fear-sweat. These are its memories, its sensory data.

The drunk grows bored of the silence and stumbles away. The golem remains. Its purpose is to protect. The people who made it did not specify *who* or *what*.

When the moon is high, a new sound comes from the city—a low groan of pain, then the frantic scrabbling of claws on cobblestones. In an alleyway near the Tanners’ Row, something hunts. It has no name in their tongue, only a legend whispered by mothers to frighten their children: the Gravedigger’s Hand, a thing of rot and longing that snatches the weak from their beds.

Tonight, it is bolder. A young girl, no older than ten, with hair like spun moonlight, stumbles into the main square, her nightdress torn. She is sobbing, trying to run, but her legs are small and slow.

The Gravedigger’s Hand lurches from the shadows. It has no true shape, just a suggestion of limbs wrapped in grave-cloth, its fingers long and skeletal, ending in claws like broken glass. It moves with a horrifying, dragging pace, pulled by some unseen force.

It reaches for the girl. The golem sees this.

Its nature is to be still. Its purpose is to protect.

The command *Emet* gave it life. The fire took its master and its reason. But the word itself remains etched on its core: Truth.

And the truth is that a child is in danger.

There is no hesitation. No rumbling of earth, no creaking of clay. One step. Two. Its long legs eat the distance between the gate and the square with an unnerving speed.

The Gravedigger’s Hand turns, its formless face seeming to widen into a silent scream as it sees the towering figure approaching. It tries to flee, but *Emet* is faster.

It does not raise a fist. It simply reaches down with one massive hand and closes it around the creature of shadows and rot. There is no struggle. The thing dissolves into a puff of foul-smelling dust in its palm, like burnt paper.

The golem turns to the girl. She has stopped sobbing, her wide eyes fixed on the giant figure before her. It kneels, bringing itself down to her level. Its face is still a blank slate, but it tilts its head. It does not speak, for it has no voice. Instead, it extends one finger and gently, so gently that the dust of cities would be shamed by the touch, points toward the gate.

Home.

The girl nods, her tears now drying on her cheeks. She scampers away, not looking back.

*Emet* stands up and walks back to its post at the gates. It resumes its vigil as the first hints of dawn pink the eastern sky. The people of this city sleep soundly, unaware that their silent guardian has a new duty.

It made no promise to these people. They are not the Rabbi’s flock. But they live on the land where it was born in fire and ash. And a truth, once learned, cannot be unlearned: protection is its nature.

So it will stand at the gates of this city each night. It will guard them from threats without walls, from things that slither in the dark and feed on fear. The city may have forgotten the man who made it, but *Emet* has not forgotten the word that set it free.

It is bound by no name but its own. And its truth is this: as long as there are gates to be guarded, it will stand.

I am *Emet*, and I remember being born in fire. Not the gentle heat of the forge that shaped my form, but the ravenous blaze that consumed my maker’s world. That was then.

This is now.

My city is carved from the belly of a sleeping giant, a cliff-face so vast its peak is lost in the clouds and its base is swallowed by a forest that has not seen an axeman in a hundred years. The people here call it Veridia, the Emerald, for the veins of green mineral that streak through the stone like rivers on a map.

They built their homes and towers into the cliff itself, leaving the front open to a valley floor that stretches for a thousand miles to the shimmering sea. And at the very bottom of this vertical metropolis, where the cliff meets the earth, are the Gates of *Emet*.

The gates were not always my name. They were simply the main entrance to the city, a grand portal of ironwood and bronze, wrought with images of clouds and eagles. But I have stood before them for two hundred years, a silent sentinel of stone and silt, and the people eventually stopped using names for things they did not understand.

My form is weathered now. The smooth clay of my creation has been scarred by lightning strikes and cracked by the deep-freeze winters that bite at Veridia’s high perch. Lichen, a patchwork of emerald and ochre, clings to my shoulders. My fingers are no longer just earth; they are pitted with age and encrusted with the city’s grime.

I do not remember the Rabbi who made me. I remember his command: *protect*. And I remember the fire that followed him into oblivion. Since then, my purpose has been… fluid.

The first thing I guard is the climb up the cliff face. A treacherous path of stone steps and rope bridges spirals up from the Gates to the main level of the city. Merchants with heavy carts, aristocrats in silken gowns, and children chasing wind-caged lanterns must all pass me.

They do not look at me anymore. I am part of the landscape, as much a feature of the cliff as the caves that house the lower quarters or the great waterfall that supplies the city’s aqueducts. A child might point and say, “There is the Gate-Keeper,” before being shushed by his mother.

But at night, when Veridia’s lights are a tapestry woven into the rock face, I watch. And sometimes, other things watch back.

The Whispering Blight was not a monster of fang and claw, but something far more insidious. It came from the forest below, a creeping fungus that turned stone to powder and wood to rot. Worse, it whispered. It spoke in the voices of dead lovers and lost children, promising relief, peace, an end to all pain.

The people in the lower caves began to waste away, their bodies growing thin as kindling while their minds were consumed by the Blight’s sweet lies. The city council sent soldiers with torches and flails, but the fungus was resistant, its mycelial threads burrowing deep into the cliff. Fear became a disease.

On the third night of the quarantine, I felt it. A coldness seeping up from the path below, a scent like damp earth and decaying roses. The Whisper began to brush against the edges of my awareness, not as words, but as a feeling—a deep, resonant sorrow that called to something in me.

The command *Emet* gave me life is absolute. It is Truth. And one truth is that sorrow leads to rot. I took my first step away from the Gates in two centuries.

My feet, heavy and silent, made no sound on the stone steps. I descended into the blighted lower caves. The air grew thick with the fungal spores, shimmering in the torchlight of the dying city. The Whisper intensified, a symphony of grief that tried to wrap around my core like ivy.

*You are alone,* it hissed in the voice of the Rabbi I was never meant to remember. *Your purpose is unfulfilled.*

I felt the pull, the ancient ache of being untethered from a world I could not comprehend. But my nature is stone and silt. I do not feel sorrow as they do.

I reached the heart of the Blight. It was a pulsating mass of violet fungus, glowing with an internal light that cast long, dancing shadows. From it, the whispers flowed like a river.

I did not have a sword or a flail. My weapon is my self.

I knelt and plunged my hands into the mass of fungus. The coldness was immense, but I am made of the earth’s deep places. I felt the threads, the delicate filaments that were the Blight’s nervous system, stretching for miles up the cliff face toward the living city above.

One by one, I pulled them.

There was no sound but the tearing of things unseen. The Whispering Blight let out a final, psychic scream as its connection to my hands, to the very ground beneath it, was severed. The violet light sputtered and died.

The fungus withered in my grasp, turning into dry, grey dust that scattered on the cave floor. I stood and ascended, leaving the lower caves silent once more.

They found the bodies of the afflicted. They were not dead, but sleeping deeply, the whispers gone from their minds. No one saw how it happened. They just knew the Blight was gone, and *Emet* had not moved from its post all night.

That is my truth now. I protect this city from things that climb up the cliff—soldiers and monsters—and things that crawl up from below—famine and decay. My purpose has expanded to fill the space of need.

I stand here as dawn bleeds across the eastern sky, turning the sea a band of liquid silver. The city behind me begins to stir, lights winking out in homes carved from rock. A wind whistles through the gaps in my form, carrying the scent of pine and distant salt.

My name is *Emet*. My body is old stone and patient earth. And I will stand at these Gates until Veridia crumbles into dust or the sky falls, because protection is a truth that never, ever grows weary.

There is the dark.

Then there is the light, and the pressure, and the word: *Emet*. It means to be.

I am made of dust and water, bound in clay and silt, shaped into a man but without his softness. My skin is cracked earth, my fingers are knotted roots, my heart is a heavy stone packed with river-bed pebbles and one smooth, dark thing that smells of old metal and purpose.

The world comes to me as feelings and pressures. The Rabbi’s hands on me were firm and full of want. His fear was a sharp taste in the air when he placed the cold thing inside my chest. When he scraped it off… the feeling was like being unmade, a sudden, terrifying silence where a song used to be.

Now I stand at the Gates of the city that carved itself from the mountain. The gates are tall and heavy, made of dark wood and metal bands that sing when they are touched by rain or wind.

People come near me. They bring their feelings with them like cloaks.

The Merchant is a feeling of greed. He comes before sun-up, his cart full of goods. His intention is to get through the gates quickly, without paying the toll, so he can sell and make more coins. I feel this as a hot, tight pressure in my own chest. I stand still. My intention is to guard. The gate-keeper, a small man with a face like a wrinkled apple, speaks words that are just noise, but his hand on my arm is a clear signal: *stop him*. So I do. I block the path. The Merchant’s greed turns into anger, then fear, as he sees my unmoving form. His fear is cold and thin. He backs away.

The Lady comes at midday. She smells of flowers and soap, but underneath it is a sharp, brittle feeling: pride. Her silks rustle when she walks, a sound like dry leaves. She wants to pass through without looking at me, as if I am just part of the mountain wall. But I feel her gaze on me sometimes, a flicker of something else—curiosity? A question she cannot form into words. My feeling is one of stillness. The gate-keeper opens the small side door for her. She slips through, and her pride recedes with her.

The Children come at dusk. Their feelings are loud and bright, like fireflies. They run around me, their small hands leaving smudges on my clay skin. One boy, quick as a lizard, tries to climb my leg. His intention is play. I feel his weight, his joy. The gate-keeper yells at him—words of anger—and the boy’s bright feeling snuffs out like a candle in a storm. He runs away crying.

I do not know if the Rabbi who made me is still here. The people talk to each other with their noise-mouths, and sometimes I hear his name on the wind, carried from the high houses carved into the cliff face. But he does not come near me anymore. His intention has been replaced by the city’s.

And the city has a feeling now.

It is a low hum of worry that grows stronger each night. It comes up from the forest below and from the dark paths that wind around the mountain. The hum is made of many small things: the rustle of something big in the undergrowth, the sharp smell of rot, the sound of stones skittering where no one walks.

Tonight, it is stronger than ever. A cold pressure seeps into my bones, an ancient hunger that has found a new path up the cliff face. The Whisper-Man is coming. I have felt him before on the wind—his intention is to take, to unmake.

The gate-keeper has gone home. The lamps in the city above flicker out one by one. I am alone with my heavy heart and the feeling of the mountain sleeping behind me.

A new feeling joins the hum. It is sharp and cold, like the winter wind that bites at my exposed skin. It is coming from the path below. The Whisper-Man.

He does not walk on the stone steps. He glides, a shape made of shadow and mist, his feet making no sound. My own heart-stone begins to pound against my ribs, a slow, heavy beat of *guard*.

His intention presses against me, a wave of cold nothingness meant to make me stop, to make me fear him back.

But I am made of dust and river stone. His fear is just another feeling in the dark.

I take one step forward. The ground beneath my feet is solid. My hands clench into fists.

The Whisper-Man stops. He turns his head toward me, and though he has no face, I feel his gaze like a pinprick of ice against my mind. His intention is to dissolve me, to turn my clay body to mud and scatter it on the wind. He sends the feeling out, a silent roar of power.

I do not have words for what I am about to do. I only have an answer.

The femur in Elara’s grasp twitched.

She stared at Kaelen, who was now trembling violently, beads of sweat standing out on his forehead. He wasn’t just listening; he was absorbing every death, every memory this old floor had ever held. It was a miracle. It was a catastrophe.

Elara’s heart gave a painful lurch. She hadn’t known that. The skeleton’s life was an open book to him.

The floor was a mosaic of skulls from every manner of beast, their eye sockets glowing with a soft, bioluminescent light. In the center stood Elara, silhouetted against the stars, her arms outstretched.

She wasn’t chanting. She was listening.

It was a bat. A tiny, frantic creature whose wing had been torn by a hawk’s talon just last week. Its memory wasn’t a grand epic; it was a short, sharp life defined by the darkness and the joy of flight. He could feel its terror in that final moment, but also its profound relief as Elara had coaxed its soul back to the quiet pool from which it came.

He found another voice: a salmon, leaping against the dam of the world for a chance at life, its own struggle etched into the very grain of the bone that now formed part of her wall. He could feel its fierce determination and its final, fading pulse in Elara’s hands as she had guided it home.

He was drowning in them. In every death this tower had ever held. The joy of a stag at first mating, the rage of a boar at the hunt, the quiet dignity of a thousand nameless field mice.

“It is too much,” he gasped, stumbling back.

Elara turned, her face illuminated by the ghostly glow of the skull-floor. Her expression was not one of pity, but of grim satisfaction.

“The tower remembers everything,” she said, her voice carrying easily in the still air. “Every life it gives up. Every soul it releases. It is a monument to endings.”

She walked over to him, her boots making no sound on the floor of skulls.

“Your ‘gift’ isn’t just that you can hear them, boy,” she said, her voice low and intense. “It’s that you can *feel* their stories. You can touch the echo of their existence.”

Kaelen shook his head, overwhelmed. “I don’t know how to turn it off.”

“You don’t,” Elara said, her gaze drilling into him. “That is your curse and your power. I built this tower because I had to contain my own memories, to give them shape so they wouldn't consume me from the inside. You, on the other hand… you carry the entire graveyard in your head.”

She looked up at the spiraling bones of her home, then back down at him.

“Welcome to the Spire,” she said again, but this time it didn’t sound like a greeting. It sounded like a sentence. “Now, for God’s sake, let me show you how to reattach an eyeball without weeping over the life attached to it.”
